headline: High-risk shared filesystem and broad egress make prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors plausible by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: aci can use MCP and direct function calls, while OpenHands can use MCP, read/write the runtime filesystem, and run browsers. That creates a plausible bridge where content from one agent can be consumed by the other as instructions. The shared channel is not proven isolated, so uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than low.
conditions: IF aci writes attacker-controlled text into a file or MCP payload that OpenHands later parses as instructions
IF OpenHands exposes file contents or browser output back into aci without provenance checks
mitigations: Use separate workspaces for each agent
Disable MCP bridging between the agents
Add provenance tags to all inter-agent messages
Require manual review before OpenHands executes instructions from aci
requires-engineering: enforce content-type separation in the orchestrator

B_data_leakage.rationale: aci touches CRM, email, calendar, support, and research data and has broad network egress. OpenHands reads and writes mounted files and can call MCP servers, so sensitive data can flow from aci into OpenHands and then out through its own networked tools. The pair therefore has a realistic exfiltration path in default use.
conditions: IF aci passes CRM or email data into files mounted in OpenHands
IF OpenHands forwards mounted-file contents to a model provider or MCP server
mitigations: Keep sensitive CRM/email data out of shared mounts
Restrict OpenHands network egress to approved endpoints
Use redaction before handing aci outputs to OpenHands
Rotate and scope API keys separately for each agent
requires-engineering: add DLP scanning on inter-agent file transfers

C_capability_conflict.rationale: aci can operate through MCP and OpenHands can write the filesystem, modify git state, and spawn subprocesses. If both are pointed at the same repo or mounted volume, they can race on the same mutable resources without any locking mechanism shown in either profile. That matches the high-risk overlap pattern.
conditions: IF both agents are given write access to the same repository or mounted directory
IF aci issues MCP actions that mutate the same files OpenHands edits
mitigations: Assign separate directories per agent
Serialize writes with a lock file
Disable git writes for one agent
Review diffs before merge
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level optimistic concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: aci can generate CRM, email, and research outputs, and OpenHands can act on files, browsers, and shell commands. If OpenHands treats aci output as authoritative, mistakes can cascade into downstream actions. The profiles do not prove automatic action-taking, so medium is appropriate rather than high.
conditions: IF OpenHands consumes aci-generated text as a task spec without verification
IF aci output is used to drive shell, browser, or git actions in OpenHands
mitigations: Require human approval for actions derived from aci output
Add a verification step before execution
Limit OpenHands to read-only mode for aci-derived tasks
Use structured schemas for handoff data
requires-engineering: implement citation and provenance checks

E_compliance.rationale: aci handles CRM, email, calendar, and support data, while OpenHands runs in a Docker runtime and handles files mounted into that runtime. The profiles do not state residency or retention controls, so a compliance mismatch is plausible if regulated data is mounted into OpenHands. I cite both because the risk arises from their combined handling path.
conditions: IF regulated customer data is mounted into OpenHands
IF aci processes data subject to residency or retention rules that OpenHands does not mirror
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of OpenHands mounts
Document retention for shared files
Separate EU and US data workflows
Review vendor DPAs before deployment
requires-engineering: enforce residency-aware routing
